PV Design Lab

Solar PV Design Lab

From sunlight to a complete PV system

Ten short lessons, each with a live simulator. Learn what every parameter means, size a system by hand, then check your design with confidence.

The six numbers behind every design

kWpInstalled DC power at STC. Everything else is sized from it.
VocOpen-circuit voltage. Highest when cold. Sets the maximum string length.
VmpVoltage at maximum power. Lowest when hot. Sets the minimum string length.
Isc, ImpCurrent. Adds up in parallel. Sets cable, fuse and inverter input limits.
PSHPeak sun hours per day, equal to daily kWh/m². Turns power into energy.
PRPerformance ratio, usually 0.75 to 0.85. One number for all real-world losses.

Your learning path

Your progress

How to study
  1. Read the short lesson, then change every slider in its lab and watch the numbers.
  2. Take the quiz on that topic. Wrong answers explain the reasoning.
  3. Run the challenges. They create new numbers every time, so you cannot memorise them.
  4. Finish with the Batteries lesson, then test yourself with the quiz and the design challenges.
Be careful with real projects

Module and inverter values in this lab are typical, not from a specific product. Always take final numbers from the manufacturer datasheet and follow your local electrical code (IEC 62548, NEC 690 or national rules).

Lesson 1 · Foundations

Cell physics and the datasheet

A solar module is a stack of small diodes that make current when light hits them. Once you see that, every datasheet number has a reason.

How a cell turns light into current

A silicon cell is a p-n junction. A photon with enough energy lifts an electron across the bandgap, 1.12 eV for silicon. The electric field at the junction pushes electrons to one side and holes to the other. Connect a load and current flows. More light creates more electron-hole pairs, so current follows irradiance. The junction sets the voltage, so a cell stays near 0.6 to 0.75 V whatever its size, and voltage falls as the cell heats up.

The cell equation every simulator uses

One-diode model I = IL − I0·(eq(V+I·Rs)/(n·k·T) − 1) − (V + I·Rs)/Rsh IL photocurrent, proportional to irradiance. I0 diode saturation current. n ideality factor. k = 1.381·10⁻²³ J/K. q = 1.602·10⁻¹⁹ C. T in kelvin. Rs series resistance, Rsh shunt resistance.

A design program fits exactly this model to your module datasheet. That is why it asks for Isc, Voc, Vmpp, Impp and the temperature coefficients, then calculates Rs, Rsh and the diode factor by itself. The Panel Lab in this app uses a simpler curve that passes exactly through the three datasheet points, which is enough to learn every behaviour.

From cell to array

Cell

0.6 to 0.75 V, 10 to 14 A for a large wafer. About 5 W.

Module

54 to 72 cells in series (half-cut cells split this in two parallel halves). 37 to 54 V, 400 to 700 W.

String

Modules in series. Voltages add, current stays the same. Typically 10 to 25 modules.

Array

Strings in parallel. Currents add, voltage stays the same.

STC

Standard Test Conditions are 1000 W/m² irradiance, 25 °C cell temperature and the AM1.5 spectrum. A roof is almost never at STC, so datasheet power is a label for comparing modules, not a promise of output.

Lesson 2 · Panel behaviour

I-V and P-V curve lab

Change sunlight, temperature and shade, and watch one module react. This single graph explains most of PV design.

Try these four experiments

1. Less light

Set irradiance to 200 W/m². Isc falls to about a fifth. Voc drops only a few volts, because voltage depends on the logarithm of light.

2. A hot roof

Set cell temperature to 65 °C. Voc and Vmp fall, Isc rises a little, and Pmax falls by about 0.3 to 0.4 % for every degree. Hot modules lose power.

3. One third in the dark

Shade one third by 100 %. A bypass diode switches that third out. Power falls to about two thirds, not to zero.

4. Partial shade

Shade one third by 60 %. The P-V curve gets two humps. A simple MPPT can lock onto the smaller one. See the Inverters lesson.

Rule to remember

Current follows light. Voltage follows temperature. That is why we check current at high irradiance and voltage at the coldest and hottest temperatures.

Current with light and heatIsc(G,T) = IscSTC·(G/1000)·[1 + α(T − 25)]G in W/m², T is cell temperature in °C, α in 1/°C.
Voltage with light and heatVoc(G,T) = VocSTC·[1 + β(T − 25)] + Ns·n·VT·ln(G/1000)VT = kT/q, about 25.7 mV at 25 °C. Ns cells in series.
Power with light and heatPmax(G,T) ≈ PSTC·(G/1000)·[1 + γ(T − 25)]γ is the Pmax temperature coefficient, negative.
Cell temperature in the fieldTcell = Tamb + (NOCT − 20)/800 · GQuick estimate. A real roof also depends on wind and mounting.

Lesson 3 · Technologies

Types of solar panel

Efficiency, temperature behaviour, ageing and price differ between technologies. Compare them with numbers, then choose for the site.

Side-by-side

TechnologyEfficiencyγ (%/°C)Year-1 lossThen per yearBest for

Typical 2025 to 2026 ranges for commercial modules. Individual products vary, so read the datasheet.

Which one should I choose?

Small roof, high demand

Pick the highest efficiency (TOPCon, HJT or back-contact). More watts per square metre.

Very hot climate

Pick the lowest |γ| (HJT, TOPCon) or CdTe. Less power lost above 25 °C.

Large ground-mount, cost per watt

TOPCon or PERC at utility scale. Consider bifacial on a tracker or high-albedo ground.

Diffuse light, weight limits, curved surfaces

Thin film or flexible modules, accepting lower efficiency.

Bifacial gain

A bifacial module also collects light on the rear. Typical rear gain is 5 to 15 %, and 20 % or more over white membranes or snow. It depends on ground reflectance (albedo), mounting height and row spacing. Flush roof mounting gives almost no gain.

Lesson 4 · Connecting modules

Series, parallel and mismatch

How you wire modules decides the array voltage and current. It also decides how badly one shaded module hurts the rest.

Series (string)

Plus of one module to minus of the next. Voltages add, current stays the same as one module. The weakest module limits the current of the whole string.

Parallel

All pluses together, all minuses together. Currents add, voltage stays the same as one string. Needs fuses once you have three or more strings.

String voltageVstr = Ns · VmpSame rule for Voc.
Array currentIarr = Np · ImpSame rule for Isc.
Array powerP = Ns · Np · PmodIgnoring mismatch and wiring loss.
Wiring rules
  • Keep modules in one string identical in model, power class, tilt and orientation.
  • Strings that share one MPPT input should have the same length. Different orientations belong on different MPPT inputs.
  • Never connect the plus of one string to the minus of another by mistake. Check Voc and polarity with a meter before connecting to the inverter.
  • Bypass diodes limit shading loss inside a module. They do not remove the need for good layout.

Lesson 5 · Power electronics

Inverters and how they work

The inverter finds the best operating point on the array curve, then turns DC into grid-quality AC. Learn the types, the stages inside, and the sizing ratio.

String inverter most common

1 to 100 kW with one to ten MPPT inputs. One inverter serves several strings. Low cost per watt, easy to service. Shading on one string affects everything on that MPPT.

Central inverter

500 kW to several MW, fed by DC combiner boxes. Used in utility plants. Few units to maintain, but one failure takes out a large block.

Microinverter

Under the module, 250 to 2000 W. Every module has its own MPPT and the roof carries only AC. Best for shaded or complex roofs. Higher cost per watt.

Power optimizer

A DC-DC unit per module feeding a simple string inverter. Module-level MPPT, monitoring and rapid shutdown, with one central inverter.

Hybrid inverter

PV input, battery charger and grid connection in one box, often with a backup output. Used for self-consumption and backup.

Off-grid inverter and charge controller

Creates its own AC supply from a battery at 12, 24 or 48 V. PV charges the battery through a PWM or MPPT charge controller, built in or separate.

Compare

FeatureStringCentralMicroOptimizer + string
Typical size1 to 100 kW0.5 to 5 MW0.25 to 2 kW per unit3 to 100 kW
MPPT levelStringWhole blockModuleModule
Shade toleranceMediumLowHighHigh
DC voltage on roofUp to 1000 or 1500 VUp to 1500 VModule voltage onlyLow and controlled
Cost per wattLowLowestHighMedium to high
Point of failureOne unitLarge blockOne moduleInverter or one optimizer
Best forMost roofs and plantsUtility scaleComplex or shaded roofsPartial shade, safety rules
Charge controllers

A PWM controller connects the array straight to the battery, so array voltage must match battery voltage. An MPPT controller converts the extra voltage into extra current and usually harvests 10 to 30 % more. Use MPPT for anything above a small 12 V system.

Inside a grid-tied inverter

  1. MPPT and boost stage. Adjusts the duty cycle so the array works at its maximum power point, and raises the voltage to the DC link.
  2. DC link. A capacitor bank holds a stable voltage (about 360 to 800 V) and absorbs the 100 Hz power ripple of single-phase AC.
  3. H-bridge. Fast switches create a train of pulses whose width follows a sine wave (PWM).
  4. Filter. Inductors and capacitors average the pulses into a clean sine wave.
  5. Grid interface. A phase-locked loop matches voltage, frequency and phase. Anti-islanding stops export during a grid outage. Residual-current and insulation monitoring protect people.
Boost converter (ideal)Vout = Vin / (1 − D)D is the switch duty cycle, 0 to 1. The MPPT moves D to move the array voltage.
PWM output (bipolar, single-phase)Vac,peak = m · Vdc,   Vac,rms = m·Vdc/√2m is the modulation index, 0 to 1. For a 230 V grid you need Vdc ≥ 325 V ÷ m.
AC powerP = Vrms · Irms · cos φGrid codes may ask for cos φ other than 1 to support the grid with reactive power.
Single-phase power ripplep(t) = Vrms·Irms·[1 − cos(2ωt)]Power pulses at twice the grid frequency. The DC link capacitor smooths it.

The maximum power point moves with sunlight and temperature, so the inverter has to keep searching. The common method is perturb and observe: change the voltage by a small step, compare the power, and keep going if it rose or reverse if it fell. It is simple and works well on a smooth curve. Under partial shade the curve has several humps, and the tracker can settle on a local one. Better inverters run an occasional global scan.

Arrays rarely reach nameplate power, because of heat, dirt, angle and losses. So designers install more DC than the inverter's AC rating. The DC/AC ratio (also called loading ratio) is typically 1.1 to 1.3. A few hours a year the inverter caps its output (clipping), but the inverter works nearer full load and costs less per kWh.

DC/AC ratioDC/AC = Parray,STC / Pinv,ACExample: 13 kWp on a 10 kW inverter gives 1.3.

Inverters convert best near the middle of their load range. A single peak number hides low-load behaviour, so datasheets add a weighted efficiency that reflects how much energy is processed at each load level.

European efficiencyηEU = 0.03η5 + 0.06η10 + 0.13η20 + 0.10η30 + 0.48η50 + 0.20η100Subscripts are the load as a percentage of rated power. Weights come from typical European sunshine.
Conversion lossPloss = Pdc − Pac = Pdc·(1 − η)At 98 % efficiency a 10 kW inverter wastes about 200 W as heat at full load.

Lesson 6 · Orientation

Sun position, tilt and row spacing

Where the sun is, and where your modules point, decides every kilowatt-hour. Test tilt and azimuth on any day of the year, then space the rows so they do not shade each other.

Solar declination (Cooper)δ = 23.45° · sin[360°·(284 + n)/365]n is the day of the year, 1 to 365. Declination swings from −23.45° to +23.45°.
Solar altitudesin α = sin φ sin δ + cos φ cos δ cos ωφ latitude, ω hour angle = 15° × (hours from solar noon).
Noon altitudeαnoon = 90° − |φ − δ|At the winter solstice in the northern hemisphere: 90° − φ − 23.45°.
Day lengthN = (2/15) · arccos(− tan φ · tan δ)   [hours]arccos in degrees.
Rule-of-thumb annual tiltβopt ≈ 3.7° + 0.69·|φ|Fixed tilt for a year-round maximum. Use |φ| − 15° for summer, |φ| + 15° for winter.
Light on the tilted planeGpoa = DNI·cos θ + DHI·(1 + cos β)/2 + ρ·GHI·(1 − cos β)/2Direct + sky diffuse + ground reflection. θ is the angle between sun rays and the module normal, ρ the albedo.
Which way to face

Face the equator: true south in the northern hemisphere, true north in the southern hemisphere. Use true, not magnetic, bearing. This lab counts azimuth from that equator-facing direction: 0° faces it, east is negative, west is positive.

Row spacing without shading

When modules are in rows on a flat roof or ground, the front row shades the one behind it when the sun is low. Size the gap for the worst case, noon at the winter solstice, or accept some winter shading for a denser layout.

Row pitch (centre to centre)D = L · [cos β + sin β / tan αw]L module length along the slope, β tilt, αw = 90° − |φ| − 23.45°.
Ground coverage ratioGCR = L / DHigher GCR means more kW per hectare but more shading and less rear gain.

Lesson 7 · Sizing

Sizing studio

Four calculators that follow the real design order: energy to array size, array to strings, off-grid storage, then cables and fuses. Every result shows the formula it used.

Start from what the customer uses. Add the daily energy of every load, divide by the sun available and by the efficiency of the whole chain.

Array sizePpv [kWp] = Eday / (PSH × PR)Eday in kWh/day. PSH = daily irradiation on the tilted plane in kWh/m² (equal to peak sun hours). PR is the performance ratio.
Number of modulesN = ⌈ Ppv · 1000 / Pmodule ⌉Round up, then adjust to fit whole strings.
Where to find PSH

Use PVGIS, NASA POWER or Global Solar Atlas for your coordinates. For off-grid design take the worst month you must cover, not the annual average. Typical PR: 0.75 to 0.85 grid-tied, 0.60 to 0.70 off-grid with batteries.

Temperature moves voltage, and the inverter has a hard upper limit and a lower working limit. Check three corners: the coldest morning (highest voltage), the hottest afternoon (lowest voltage), and the current limits.

Highest voltage (coldest)Voc,cold = Voc·[1 + β·(Tmin − 25)]β in 1/°C, negative, so the result is higher than STC. Tmin is the record low ambient, which equals cell temperature at dawn.
Maximum modules per stringNmax = ⌊ Vlimit / Voc,cold ⌋Vlimit is the lower of inverter max DC voltage and module max system voltage.
Lowest working voltage (hottest)Vmp,hot = Vmp·[1 + βVmp·(Tcell,max − 25)]βVmp is about γ − α. If it is not on the datasheet, use γ − α.
Minimum modules per stringNmin = ⌈ VMPPT,min / Vmp,hot ⌉Also make N × Voc(hot) larger than the inverter start voltage.
Strings per MPPT inputNp = ⌊ Imax,in / Imp ⌋ and ⌊ Isc,max,in / Isc ⌋Take the smaller. Higher irradiance can add 10 to 25 % over STC current in cold, clear weather.
Upper MPPT checkN · Vmp,cold ≤ VMPPT,maxNot a hard limit. Above it the inverter just limits power on cold bright mornings.

An off-grid system has to cover the load on bad days and at night. Size the battery for days of autonomy, size the array to refill it, and size the controller to carry the current.

Battery energyEbat = Eday · Daut / (ηinv · DoD)Daut days of autonomy, DoD usable depth of discharge, ηinv inverter efficiency.
Battery capacityC [Ah] = Ebat [Wh] / VbatSeries cells set the voltage, parallel strings set the Ah.
Charge controller currentIcc = 1.25 · Ppv / Vbat25 % safety margin. Use the next standard rating up.
Controller voltage checkNs · Voc,cold ≤ Vcc,maxSame cold-morning rule as for inverters.
Typical usable depth of discharge

Lead-acid (flooded or AGM): 50 %. Gel: 50 to 60 %. Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄): 80 to 90 %. Going deeper shortens battery life.

Cables should carry the current safely and lose little power. Design for 1 to 2 % loss on DC strings and about 1 to 3 % on AC, and choose fuses from the module datasheet.

Voltage drop (DC, two conductors)ΔV = 2 · L · I · ρ / AL one-way length in m, I current in A, A cross-section in mm², ρ resistivity: 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m for copper at 20 °C.
Resistivity with temperatureρ(T) = ρ₂₀ · [1 + 0.00393 · (T − 20)]Copper. Roof cables run at 60 to 70 °C, so resistance is about 20 % higher.
Design currentIdesign = 1.25 · IscSafety factor for high irradiance. Cable ampacity must also be derated for temperature and grouping, and NEC adds another 1.25.
String fuse rating1.4 to 1.56 × Isc ≤ Ifuse ≤ Imax series fuseLower bound depends on the code in force (NEC 690: 1.56). The upper bound is on the module datasheet.

Lesson 8 · On site

Installation, mounting and protection

How modules attach to the structure, how the electrical chain is protected, and what to test before switching on.

Mounting types

Pitched roof

Hooks or brackets fixed to rafters, aluminium rails, mid and end clamps. Needs flashing for weatherproofing and a structural check of the roof.

Flat roof

Tilted frames held by ballast blocks or mechanical anchors. Low tilt (10 to 15°) allows tight row spacing and lowers wind load.

Ground mount

Driven piles, ground screws or concrete footings. Easy to set the ideal tilt and orientation. Needs fencing and drainage.

Carport or canopy

Steel structure over parking. Produces power and shade. Higher structure cost per kW.

Single-axis tracker

Rotates east to west. Adds roughly 15 to 25 % energy at extra cost and maintenance. Utility scale.

Building-integrated

Modules replace roof or facade material. Lower yield because of angle and ventilation, but dual use.

Fixing the array against wind

Wind pushes down on the front face and tries to lift the array from behind. Uplift decides the number and strength of anchors or the ballast mass. Real designs follow a wind code (Eurocode 1, ASCE 7 or the national standard), which gives pressure coefficients by roof zone. The calculator here shows the order of magnitude.

Dynamic wind pressureq = ½ · ρair · v²ρair = 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level, v in m/s. Pressure in Pa.
Force on the arrayF = q · Cf · ACf net pressure coefficient, about 1 to 2.5 depending on tilt and roof zone, A module area.
Load per anchorFanchor = SF · Fuplift / nSF safety factor, typically 1.5.
Ballast per modulemballast = SF · Fuplift / g − mmoduleFriction and dead load of the frame help, so real values need the supplier's tables.

Electrical chain and protection

Checklists

Before you build: site survey
  • Roof structure, age and waterproofing. Free area after setbacks and obstructions.
  • Shading from trees, chimneys and neighbouring buildings through the year (horizon and near objects).
  • Orientation, tilt, available cable routes, inverter location with ventilation.
  • Grid connection point, supply voltage, utility rules and metering.
Installation good practice
  • Use the same connector brand and type on both halves. Mixed brands cause hot connections.
  • Keep DC cable loops small, secure cables off sharp edges and out of standing water, and use UV-resistant PV cable.
  • Tighten clamps and bolts to the torque in the manual. Avoid mixing metals that cause galvanic corrosion.
  • Leave air space behind modules. Every 10 °C cooler gives roughly 3 to 4 % more power.
  • Label all isolators, strings and warning notices. Fit rapid shutdown where the code requires it.
Commissioning tests
  1. Visual inspection of structure, connectors and cable routing.
  2. Measure Voc and polarity of each string before closing the isolator. It should match N × Voc corrected for temperature, within about 3 to 5 %.
  3. Measure Isc if the procedure allows, and compare strings in the same irradiance.
  4. Insulation resistance test of the DC circuit, and earth continuity of all metal parts.
  5. Set the inverter grid code and country. Check power, voltage and frequency on first start.
  6. Thermal image under load for hot connections. Record all results in the handover file.
Safety

DC cannot be switched off at the module while the sun is up. Never open DC connectors under load, because the arc can be sustained. Work at height needs fall protection. Only qualified electricians connect to the AC supply.

Lesson 9 · Performance

Energy yield and system losses

The nameplate is only the start. Soiling, heat, wiring, shade and conversion take a share before the energy reaches the meter.

Annual energyE = PkWp · Hpoa · PRHpoa in kWh/m² per year on the module plane. Each full-sun hour is 1 kWh/m².
Performance ratioPR = E / (PkWp · Hpoa) = ∏ (1 − lossi)Dimensionless. Good systems reach 0.78 to 0.86.
Specific yieldYf = E / PkWp = Hpoa · PR   [kWh/kWp/yr]The number to compare sites and designs. Typical range is 900 to 2000 depending on climate.
Capacity factorCF = E / (PAC · 8760)For a fixed array it is about 12 to 25 %.

Lesson 10 · Putting it together

Your first PVsyst project

A PVsyst study is a fixed sequence of decisions. This lesson lists them in order, shows which field takes which number, and builds a complete design with a parameter sheet you can type in.

The workflow

1 · Create the project and the site

Choose Grid-connected or Stand-alone. Set the geographical site: latitude, longitude, altitude, time zone. Import meteorological data (Meteonorm, NASA, PVGIS or your own file). Check that annual GHI and temperatures look right against a second source, because every result depends on this file.

2 · Variant and orientation

Pick the plane type (fixed tilted plane, sheds, trackers, and so on) and enter tilt and azimuth. In PVsyst azimuth 0° faces the equator, east is negative and west positive, the same convention as the Sun lab here. Compare tilts and read the loss against the optimum. Set the ground albedo (about 0.2 for grass, 0.6 to 0.8 for snow) if you use bifacial modules.

3 · System definition

Select the module and inverter from the databases, or import the manufacturer's PAN and OND files. Enter planned power or the number of modules, then modules in series and strings in parallel. PVsyst draws the array voltage window: Voc at the lowest temperature against the inverter maximum, and Vmpp at high temperature against the MPPT minimum. It also shows the Pnom ratio, which is the DC/AC ratio, and warns about overvoltage, undervoltage and current overload.

4 · Detailed losses

Set the thermal loss factors (a free-standing array ventilates well, an integrated roof does not), ohmic wiring loss from cable length and size, soiling, module quality and light-induced degradation, mismatch, incidence angle effect (IAM), auxiliaries and unavailability. Start from typical values and justify each one in a report.

5 · Horizon and near shading

Import a horizon profile for distant hills. Build a 3D scene for nearby objects, chimneys, trees and the other rows, then run the shading calculation. Use the row-spacing calculator in the Sun lesson to set the starting pitch.

6 · Run and read the result

Look at produced energy, specific production in kWh/kWp/year and performance ratio, then the loss diagram. Compare the energy with your hand calculation from the Yield lesson. If they differ by more than about 5 %, find which loss is different. Finally export the PDF report.

Off-grid projects

Choose Stand-alone system. Define the daily and seasonal user needs, the battery pack and the controller. PVsyst reports the loss of load fraction and unused energy. Increase battery or array size until the loss of load meets your target.

What the warnings mean

WarningCauseFix
Array voltage too highN × Voc at the lowest temperature exceeds the inverter or module limitFewer modules per string
Vmpp below MPPT minimumString too short for hot afternoonsMore modules per string, or an inverter with a lower MPPT range
Input current above inverter limitToo many strings on one MPPTSpread strings over more MPPT inputs, or use a bigger inverter
High overload lossDC/AC ratio too high, so peak power is clippedLarger inverter or fewer modules
Pnom ratio under 1Inverter larger than the arrayUsually fine, but check if a smaller inverter saves cost
